name: Fibonacci / 1D DP
description: The simplest DP pattern where each state depends on the previous one or two states. Foundation for understanding DP. Used for climbing stairs, house robber base case, and any problem where the answer to n depends on n-1 and/or n-2.

examples.title: Example 1: Climbing Stairs (Fibonacci Variant)
examples.explanation: To reach step n, you can come from n-1 (1 step) or n-2 (2 steps). So ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2). This is Fibonacci. Iterative uses O(1) space. Time O(n), Space O(1) or O(n) for memo.

examples.title: Example 2: House Robber (Non-Adjacent Sum)
examples.explanation: At house i, either skip it (keep dp[i-1]) or rob it (dp[i-2] + current house value). Can't rob adjacent. State only depends on two previous values, so O(1) space. Time O(n), Space O(1).

name: 0/1 Knapsack
description: Given items with weight and value, pick a subset with total weight <= W that maximizes total value. Each item can be taken at most once. The classic combinatorial optimization problem and foundation for many DP variants.

examples.title: Example 1: Subset Sum (Decision Version)
examples.explanation: dp[j] = can we reach sum j using seen items? For each number, iterate backwards (important!) so we don't reuse the same item. Time O(n * target), Space O(target).

examples.title: Example 2: 0/1 Knapsack (Max Value)
examples.explanation: dp[i][w] = max value considering first i items with capacity w. Include: add value and reduce capacity. Skip: keep previous best. Backwards iteration in 1D prevents item reuse. Time O(n*W), Space O(W).

name: Unbounded Knapsack
description: Like 0/1 knapsack, but each item can be used unlimited times. Used for coin change, rod cutting, and problems where you can reuse elements. The inner loop iterates forward (not backward) because items can be reused.

examples.title: Example 1: Coin Change (Minimum Coins)
examples.explanation: dp[i] = min coins needed for amount i. For each coin <= i, try using it and add 1 to dp[i-coin]. Initialize with amount+1 as infinity. Forward iteration because coins are unlimited. Time O(amount * coins), Space O(amount).

examples.title: Example 2: Perfect Squares (Lagrange's Theorem variant)
examples.explanation: dp[i] = min squares summing to i. For each square <= i, try subtracting it. Unbounded because same square can be used multiple times (e.g., 12 = 4+4+4). Time O(n * sqrt(n)), Space O(n).

name: Longest Common Subsequence (LCS)
description: Finds the longest subsequence common to two strings. A subsequence doesn't need to be contiguous. This 2D DP pattern is the basis for edit distance, string matching, and diff algorithms.

examples.title: Example 1: Standard LCS Length
examples.explanation: If chars match: dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]. If not: max of skipping char from text1 (dp[i-1][j]) or text2 (dp[i][j-1]). 2D table where rows represent text1 prefixes, columns represent text2 prefixes. Time O(m*n), Space O(m*n) or O(n).

examples.title: Example 2: Edit Distance (Levenshtein)
examples.explanation: LCS variant with three operations: insert, delete, replace. If chars match, cost is 0 (inherit diagonal). Otherwise, take min of three neighbors plus 1. Time O(m*n), Space O(m*n).

name: Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS)
description: Finds the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. Classic DP with a binary search optimization that reduces time from O(n^2) to O(n log n). Used for Russian Doll Envelopes and patience sorting variants.

examples.title: Example 1: DP O(n^2) with Reconstruction
examples.explanation: dp[i] is the LIS length ending at position i. For each i, look at all j < i. If nums[j] < nums[i], we can extend that subsequence. Track prev[] to reconstruct the actual sequence. Time O(n^2), Space O(n).

examples.title: Example 2: Binary Search O(n log n) Optimization
examples.explanation: tails array maintains the smallest possible ending value for increasing subsequences of each length. Binary search finds where to place current num. If num is larger than all tails, extend. Otherwise, replace to keep tails minimal. Time O(n log n), Space O(n).

name: Palindrome DP
description: Problems involving palindromic substrings or subsequences. Uses 2D DP where dp[i][j] represents whether substring s[i..j] is a palindrome or the length of the longest palindromic subsequence in that range.

examples.title: Example 1: Longest Palindromic Substring (Expand Around Center - O(1) Space)
examples.explanation: Expand around center: treat each position (and gap) as palindrome center. Odd centers check i,i. Even centers check i,i+1. DP approach fills table by length, checking edges and inner substring. Expand is O(1) space, DP is O(n^2). Both O(n^2) time.

examples.title: Example 2: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
examples.explanation: dp[i][j] = longest palindromic subsequence in s[i..j]. If s[i]==s[j], they can be outer chars of palindrome (add 2 to inner). Otherwise, max of excluding left or right char. Iterate i backwards because dp[i][j] depends on dp[i+1][*]. Time O(n^2), Space O(n^2) or O(n).

name: Matrix / Grid DP
description: DP on 2D grids where each cell's value depends on its top and/or left neighbors. Used for unique paths, minimum path sum, and grid-based game problems. Typically tabulated row by row.

examples.title: Example 1: Unique Paths (Grid Navigation)
examples.explanation: dp[i][j] = ways to reach cell (i,j). Only moves: right or down. To get to (i,j), we must come from (i-1,j) or (i,j-1). Base cases: first row/column have 1 path each. Time O(m*n), Space O(m*n) or O(n) with rolling array.

examples.title: Example 2: Minimum Path Sum
examples.explanation: dp[i][j] = min path sum to reach cell (i,j). Can only come from top or left. Initialize first row/column with cumulative sums. Time O(m*n), Space O(m*n) or O(n) with 1D rolling array (just need previous row).

name: DP on Trees
description: Applies DP principles to tree structures where each node's state depends on its children. Common patterns include robbing houses on a binary tree (can't rob adjacent nodes) and calculating maximum path sums.

examples.title: Example 1: House Robber III (Tree DP with States)
examples.explanation: For each node, return two values: rob it or don't. If rob: add node.val + skip children. If skip: take max(rob, skip) from each child. Post-order DFS ensures children are processed first. Time O(n), Space O(h) for call stack.

examples.title: Example 2: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
examples.explanation: At each node, compute best gain from left and right (clamped to 0). New path through node = node.val + left + right. Update global max. Return only one side to parent (path can't branch both ways going up). Time O(n), Space O(h).
